n: Just past the summit of the Mount of Olives, Ziba, Mephibosheth’s steward, meets David with donkeys loaded with food and wine — a generous and well-timed gift.

f.g: Probably cakes of figs or dates.

n: Ziba explains that the donkeys are for the king’s family to ride, and the food and wine are for the weary travelers.
When David asks about Mephibosheth, Ziba claims his master stayed in Jerusalem hoping to get Saul’s kingdom back. Later Mephibosheth will deny this, so Ziba’s story may be a self-serving lie.

f.w: To day shall the house of Israel restore me the kingdom of my father

n: In a hasty decision made under stress, David gives all of Mephibosheth’s property to Ziba without hearing the other side. Ziba humbly thanks him.

f.w: thine are all that pertained unto Mephibosheth

n: At Bahurim, Shimei, a relative of Saul, comes out cursing David as he passes.
He throws stones at David and his men even though they are surrounded by armed guards — a bold act of hatred.

f.g: Throwing stones was a sign of contempt and a symbolic curse.

n: Shimei calls David a man of bloodshed and a worthless scoundrel.

f.g: A man guilty of shedding blood.
Belial = worthlessness; a wicked, good-for-nothing person.

n: He accuses David of taking Saul’s throne through violence and says God is now paying him back. The charge is unfair regarding Saul, though David did carry real guilt for Uriah’s blood.

f.w: all the blood of the house of Saul

n: Abishai, quick to violence like his brother Joab, asks permission to cut off Shimei’s head.
David rebukes Abishai. Perhaps the Lord has sent Shimei to curse him — who is David to stop it? David humbly accepts the rebuke as possibly deserved.

f.w: What have I to do with you
f.g: An idiom: “What do we have in common?” — “Stay out of this.”

n: If his own son wants him dead, why be surprised at a Benjamite’s anger? David chooses to leave Shimei alone.

f.w: my son, which came forth of my bowels
f.g: My own son, my own flesh and blood.
From the tribe of Benjamin, Saul’s tribe.

n: David hopes the Lord will see his suffering and turn the curse into a blessing. He trusts God to vindicate him rather than taking revenge.

f.w: the LORD will look on mine affliction

n: Shimei follows along the hillside, cursing, throwing stones, and flinging dust as David walks on in silence.

f.g: Throwing dust was a sign of contempt or a curse.

n: David and his weary followers finally reach a place to rest and refresh themselves, probably near the Jordan.

f.g: Some ancient versions read “came to the Jordan.”

n: Meanwhile Absalom enters Jerusalem with his supporters and his chief adviser, Ahithophel.
Hushai, David’s friend, greets Absalom with “Long live the king!” — carefully never saying which king.

f.g: Hebrew “May the king live!” — a royal acclamation (1 Samuel 10:24).

n: Absalom is suspicious and taunts Hushai for abandoning his friend David.
Hushai’s answer is cleverly ambiguous: he will serve whomever the Lord and the people have chosen. Readers know the Lord’s chosen king is David.

f.w: whom the LORD, and this people, and all the men of Israel, choose

n: He says he will serve the son just as he served the father — words Absalom hears as loyalty.
Absalom asks Ahithophel for advice on what to do next.

Ahithophel advises Absalom to take his father’s concubines publicly. This would be a claim to David’s throne and an act so offensive that there could be no reconciliation, binding his followers to him.

f.w: Go in unto thy father's concubines

f.g: Made yourself hateful to your father — a complete break.

n: A tent is set up on the palace roof and Absalom does this publicly — on the very roof where David first saw Bath-sheba. Nathan’s prophecy is fulfilled exactly.

f.w: upon the top of the house
in the sight of all Israel

n: The narrator explains that Ahithophel’s advice was so respected that people treated it like a word from God. That makes the coming defeat of his counsel all the more remarkable.

f.g: Literally “the word of God” — as if inquiring of the Lord through a priest or prophet.
